title: IRDAI's Insurance Commission Overhaul Sparks Fears for One Million Brokers' Jobs
excerpt: The regulator wants to cap commissions and cut insurers' expense limits by a third; brokers say the maths will kill jobs and leave small-town customers unserved.
body:
• IRDAI has floated a consultation paper proposing more than 30 separate commission caps by product and channel, plus a one-third cut in insurers' overall expense limits over five years. Views are open until Oct. 25, 2026.
  • The brokers' body IBAI warns the caps could put more than a million livelihoods at risk: brokers sponsor 14.81 lakh of India's 27.18 lakh point-of-sale persons, mostly self-employed in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns.
  • IRDAI's case: commissions have outrun premiums — general-insurance broker commissions jumped 173% from FY23 to FY25 while broker-placed premiums grew just 37%.
  • Nothing changes for existing policyholders yet; the paper is a proposal, and IBAI wants caps confined to coerced-choice sales rather than the whole industry.

India's insurance regulator has put the industry's economics on the table with a sweeping proposal to cap commissions and slash expense limits — and the country's insurance brokers say more than a million livelihoods could be at stake.

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) released a consultation paper titled "Reforms for Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution" last week. Its central instruments are more than 30 separate commission caps by product and channel, together with a roughly one-third reduction in insurers' overall expense-of-management (EoM) limits over five years. For life insurers the EoM ceiling would fall to 15% of premium within two years and 12.5% within five; for general insurers the glide path runs from 25% to 20%. The paper also targets mis-selling, digital "dark patterns" and compulsory bundling of insurance with loans. IRDAI has invited views until Oct. 25, 2026.

The brokers' case: jobs and choice at risk

The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI), the apex body for licensed brokers, responded with a stark warning: the proposal, it said, would harm the very policyholders it seeks to protect.

"Commission caps where the intermediary earns below the cost of serving these customers will end up reaching these customers, defeating the very objective of this reform."

— Insurance Brokers Association of India

IBAI's numbers underline the scale of the workforce at issue. As of March 31, 2025, brokers sponsored 14.81 lakh of India's 27.18 lakh point-of-sale persons and 16,230 of 26,316 motor insurance service providers — most of them self-employed in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns — plus the professionals employed directly by broking firms. If commissions fall below the cost of serving these markets, IBAI argues, brokers will simply stop reaching them, leaving small-town customers worse off, not better.

The association also questions the paper's reading of its own data. Total expenses of management in general insurance actually fell from 28.2% of premium in FY2022-23 to 26.5% in FY2024-25 while premiums grew about 13% a year, IBAI points out, adding that the paper leans on outlying commission and margin figures that do not represent industry averages. The great majority of brokers, it says, operate on modest margins, and genuine overcharging where customers have little choice should be handled through fair-conduct rules.

IBAI further argues the proposal breaks with the regulator's own stance since brokers were introduced in 2002: the paper would pay a customer's own broker less than the insurer's tied agent, "overriding" the policyholder's choice of adviser. On global practice, the association notes that 18 of the world's 20 largest non-life markets impose no commission caps on commercial lines, and that India's own experiment with caps between 2002 and 2023 produced disguised payments and tax non-compliance that the 2023 reform resolved.

The regulator's case: commissions running ahead of premiums

IRDAI's figures, though, tell a story of distribution economics drifting away from policyholders. Between FY23 and FY25, general-insurance premiums placed through brokers rose 37% — from Rs 74,460 crore to Rs 1,01,862 crore — while broker commissions including rewards leapt 173%, from Rs 6,348 crore to Rs 17,348 crore. In life insurance, premiums collected via corporate agents grew 28% while commissions rose 125%. The regulator's position is that too many products are sold on the basis of the commission behind them rather than the value in them.

Market analysts are split on the fallout. Brokerages including Bernstein and Jefferies have observed that the cuts could compress revenue and margins for independent brokers and agency networks, even as reduced distribution friction eventually fosters more competitive pricing for buyers. Insurance stocks wobbled when the paper landed.

What's next

IBAI is urging IRDAI to retain the 2023 expense framework with tighter computation rules if needed, and to confine any commission caps to credit-linked and other coerced-choice sales, where the paper's evidence of excessive remuneration is strongest. The consultation closes Oct. 25, 2026, after which IRDAI will frame final regulations — a process that could take months. For policyholders, including NRIs holding Indian life and health policies, nothing changes for now; the longer-term question is whether leaner distribution economics translate into cheaper premiums, or into thinner broker networks in the smaller towns where insurance penetration is lowest.
